title: Propositional logic: connectives and truth tables
note: Truth-functional logic builds compound sentences from simple ones with connectives: not (¬), and (∧), or (∨), if-then (→), and if and only if (↔). A compound's truth depends only on the truth of its parts, and a truth table lists every combination. 'Or' is inclusive, and a conditional is false only when its antecedent is true and its consequent false.

read.title: Reading a truth table
text: Propositional logic treats whole statements as units. Letters such as P and Q stand for simple sentences, and connectives combine them. The key idea is truth-functionality: the truth value of the compound depends only on the truth values of its parts.

A truth table shows this by listing every possible combination. With two letters there are four rows; each new letter doubles the count, so three letters need eight. A conjunction, P ∧ Q, is true only in the row where both are true. A disjunction, P ∨ Q, is false only in the row where both are false; logic's 'or' is inclusive, so it is true when both parts are true.

The conditional, P → Q, surprises beginners. It is false in just one row, where P is true and Q is false. Think of it as a promise: 'If you finish your homework, you can play.' The promise is broken only if you finish and are still not allowed to play. If you never finish, the promise is not broken, whatever happens.

Truth tables also sort sentences. A tautology is true in every row, a contradiction is false in every row, and anything else is contingent. Two sentences are equivalent when their columns match in every row.

q.q: How many rows does a truth table with three letters need?
In the homework promise, when is the conditional false?
o: When you never finish your homework
When you finish but are not allowed to play
When you finish and are allowed to play

q.q: Two sentences are logically equivalent when
o: Their truth-table columns match in every row
